paragraphs: Performance is a feature — especially for marketing sites and SaaS dashboards where every second of load time affects conversion. At Canopy Arc, we treat performance as a requirement from sprint one, not a polish task before launch.
Start with images: use modern formats, explicit dimensions, and lazy loading below the fold. Next.js Image handles much of this, but only if your layout and CMS workflows are set up correctly.
Server Components reduce client JavaScript by default. Audit what truly needs interactivity — carousels, forms, and dashboards do; static content does not. Split client boundaries deliberately.
Measure with real tools: Core Web Vitals in the field, Lighthouse in CI, and bundle analysis on every major dependency add. Set budgets and fail builds when they regress.
The goal is not perfect scores — it is a fast, stable experience on mid-range devices and average networks. That is what your users actually feel.
A design system should make the right thing easy. Without governance, it becomes another library nobody uses — or worse, three competing libraries across teams.
Start with tokens: color, spacing, typography, and radii defined once and consumed everywhere. Tailwind CSS v4 and CSS variables make this practical in modern web stacks.
Components should solve repeated product problems, not abstract every possible variant on day one. Ship Button, Input, Card, and Modal well before you debate a 47-prop DataTable.
Document usage, not just API. Designers and engineers need examples of correct patterns — especially for empty states, errors, and loading.
Review the system quarterly. Prune unused pieces, align with brand updates, and measure adoption. A living system beats a frozen specification every time.
Demos are easy. Production AI is hard. The gap is evaluation, guardrails, cost control, and failure modes users never see in a prototype.
Define success metrics before you integrate a model: accuracy on representative inputs, latency p95, cost per request, and escalation rate to humans.
Never trust a single prompt version in production. Version prompts, log inputs and outputs (with privacy controls), and A/B test changes on a slice of traffic.
Build fallbacks: when confidence is low, ask a clarifying question or route to a deterministic path. Silent wrong answers destroy trust faster than honest limits.
Security matters — prompt injection, data leakage, and over-permissioned tools are real risks. Treat AI features like any other surface that handles user data.
MVPs should be small, not sloppy. The art is choosing which shortcuts are reversible and which become expensive within six months.
Use a boring, well-understood stack for v1. Novelty belongs in the product idea, not in your auth layer or database choice.
Modular boundaries early — even a monolith can have clear domains (billing, users, core workflow) so you can extract services later without a rewrite.
Write tests for critical paths: signup, payment, and the one workflow that defines your product. Skip exhaustive coverage of admin screens that will change weekly.
Document decisions in ADRs or a simple decisions log. Future you will forget why you chose Postgres over Firebase — and that context saves hours.
Cloud bills creep. Unused staging environments, oversized instances, and unoptimized assets add up quietly until finance asks questions.
Right-size first: metrics over guesses. CPU, memory, and request patterns should drive instance types — not the largest option that feels safe.
Automate off-hours scaling for non-production. Many teams run full-size staging 24/7 with zero benefit.
CDN and caching are cheaper than compute. Push static assets to the edge, cache API responses where business rules allow, and compress aggressively.
Review monthly with owners. Assign cost visibility per environment and per service so optimization is everyone's job, not a once-a-year audit.
B2B users are busy and often expert in their domain — not yours. Interfaces should respect their time with density, clarity, and keyboard-friendly flows.
Onboarding should get users to value in minutes. Defer advanced configuration; show a working default path first.
Dashboards need hierarchy: primary KPIs above the fold, drill-down on demand, and exports where workflows leave the browser.
Empty states are opportunities — explain what will appear, why it matters, and the one action that populates the view.
Consistency beats novelty in enterprise tools. Reuse patterns across modules so learning one screen teaches ten others.
